## Keep or rush

In class order. Planned total 80 of the 80 minutes, with no slack, so
time comes from the last discussion.

| Item | Min | | If short |
|---|---:|---|---|
| To start: one ethical issue in data science that concerns you; from memory, what power depends on and which way selection pushes an estimate | 6 | Rush | The recall question only, three answers from the room |
| Problem 1: what a field's literature looks like (Ioannidis 2005); answers not revealed yet | 12 | Keep | (a) and (b); take (c), what the formula shows and what it does not, with the room at the reveal |
| Discussion break: causes of the replication crisis, cultural and statistical | 10 | Keep | One cultural and one statistical cause from two groups |
| Coding A.1 to A.3 and B.1 to B.3 | 24 | Keep | Part A in ten minutes at most; push everyone to B.2 and B.3 |
| Reveal: problem 1 and the code; the two survivor histograms side by side | 7 | Keep | The two histograms, and B.2's 0.16 against 0.19 said aloud |
| Discussion: ethical impacts; what data scientists can do; the settings | 15 | Rush; cut first | Prompts 1 and 2 with the room; prompt 3 only if there is time; prompt 4 as a fallback |
| To finish: one written sentence on p-hacking, cause and fix | 3 | Keep | |
| The task for next time | 3 | Keep | Read the task aloud |

: {tbl-colwidths="[32,6,16,46]"}

Minimum class, about 60 minutes: problem 1, the break, coding A.1 to
A.3 and B.1 to B.3 with the reveal, the closing sentence and the task
for next time. If coding runs over, take the time from discussion
prompt 3, not from the break or from prompts 1 and 2.

## If you read on

How it runs

- The exercises at the top of the sheet (1 to 3) are for students' own
  time, and coding A.4 and B.4 are practice. Say so. No marks are
  attached to any of it. (Until 19 October the in-class problems were
  1(a), 2(a) and 3(a)--(b); the convenor's convention of that day made
  problems 1 to 3 exercises and the old problem 4 the class's problem.)
- Problem 1 is attempted before anything is revealed; its solution and
  the code are revealed together, after the coding.

What the class works that the lecture only stated

All three are in the notes, so a student who misses the class has a
reference.

- **Coding A.** The lecture asked for a prediction of the survivors'
  mean. The class builds the survivors' distribution and checks the
  formula. Notes: "The filter on its own".
- **Coding B.2.** The lecture said $1 - 0.95^k$. The class finds about
  0.16, not the independent-tests figure 0.19, because the four
  $p$-values are dependent. Say that aloud when revealing.
- **Problem 1.** One slide in the lecture; derived in the notes under
  "How much of the crisis does selection alone explain?". The class adds
  what the formula shows and does not show, and which ingredient is about
  who is in the data. The calculation is Ioannidis's (2005).

Where they get stuck

1. **"Reproducibility" and "replication" used interchangeably.** The notes
   define replication in one sentence. Do not spend time on it unless a
   group builds an argument on the confusion.
2. **"p-values can be significant at some sample sizes and not others."**
   Half right. Larger $n$ at the same $\mu$ raises $\theta$. The wrong
   version is that the same data can be made significant by choosing $n$
   after the fact; that is a stopping rule and belongs with exercise 1(b).
   Redirect to $\theta = \mu\sqrt n/\sigma$.
3. **"p-hacking is fraud."** The lecture's point is that the filter
   distorts the literature with honest tests. Students who arrive with
   "cause: incentives; fix: pre-registration" have skipped the mechanism.
   Exercise 1(b) and the closing sentence are where to make them say what
   pre-registration changes (the reported comparison) and what it does
   not (power).
4. **"Correlation is not causation" as the explanation of
   non-replication.** A confounded effect replicates perfectly well; that
   failure comes later in the course. This week's failures are about
   selection.
5. **No direction on the bias.** "Away from the truth" is not an answer.
   Upward in magnitude, always, under a magnitude filter.
6. **Exercise 3(c).** The common wrong answer is "bias" alone. The size of the bias
   is set by the variance, through the power. The sentence to get out of
   them: "the file-drawer effect turns variance into bias."

On the screen

- During problem 1: its three ingredients ($p$, $\alpha$ and the power) and nothing else.
- During coding: the `generate_data()` / `one_experiment()` block.
- At the reveal: the two survivor histograms side by side. The
  $\theta = 1$ survivors look like the null survivors.
- During discussion: if the room uses a shared document, do not tidy it.

Discussion prompt 3, if reached

- Closed funds: survivorship; advertised returns biased upward; the
  platform benefits.
- Most-improved schools: selection on the extreme, and regression to the
  mean; the same schools look worse next year. Let them find it.
- Surgeons with 50+ operations: the one where direction is not obvious.
  Selection is on volume, not outcome. Volume may correlate with case
  difficulty or with skill, in either direction. A filter biases the
  outcome only if it depends on the outcome or on something correlated
  with it.
- Hired candidates: the rejected are unobserved. Who is in the data.
- Top-ten posts: selection on the extreme of a large group. What you see
  says more about the size and variance of the group's output than about
  its center.

Notation

$\mu$ is the effect, $\theta = \mu/\mathrm{se}$ the standardized effect.
$p$ in problem 1 is the prevalence of true hypotheses among those tested;
do not write it as $\pi$.

## References

- Ioannidis, John P. A., "Why Most Published Research Findings Are
  False" (*PLoS Medicine* 2(8), 2005, e124),
  <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124>.
